For years, we lied to browsers. We told them how large images on the page would be, even though we often didn't know ourselves. Browsers believed us and downloaded data based on our estimates. With the `sizes="auto"` attribute, however, we are finally offloading this calculation directly to the browser.

## Combining srcset and sizes \=== HTMHell

Responsive images are nothing new. The combination of the srcset and sizes attributes has allowed us for years to offer the browser multiple image sizes and let it pick the most suitable one.

Let's remind ourselves how it works in code:

```html
<img
  src="image-800.webp"
  srcset="
    image-400.webp 400w,
    image-800.webp 800w,
    image-1200.webp 1200w,
    image-1600.webp 1600w
  "
  sizes="
    (max-width: 600px) 100vw,
    (max-width: 1200px) calc(50vw - 20px),
    400px
  "
  width="800"
  height="600"
  alt="Example"
>
```

* srcset defines which image variants are available, and using the w descriptor we specify the actual width of the image (there is also a descriptor for [pixel density](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/img#srcset)).  
  *In the example, we have images 400, 800, 1200, and 1600 pixels wide.*

* sizes, on the other hand, specifies how wide the image is in the current layout. It is typically combined with media queries so that we can cover responsive variants as well.  
  *In the example, we state that up to a 600 px viewport width the image occupies 100% of the layout, up to 1200 px half of it minus a 20px gap, and above 1200 px it has a fixed width of 400 px.*

So where's the catch? There are simply too many magic numbers that need to be aligned.

### Hell from a performance architect's perspective

On paper, it works fine. In practice, CSS controls the layout, so manually setting all kinds of dimensions and numbers in HTML often slows down the website.

The resulting HTML is created by combining content from WYSIWYG editors and data wired up by developers. A chapter unto themselves are "smart" components like next/image that hide implementation details.

Simply put, nobody checks the final HTML structure and browser behavior, leading to the following issues:

* If sizes declares a width larger than reality, the browser needlessly downloads a huge file. This clogs the network and degrades performance metrics.
* Conversely, if you underestimate the width, your designer will complain about blurry images.
* A reusable UI component doesn't know in advance which container it will end up in. Proper configuration requires complex parameter passing in code.
* The final HTML ballooned because it needed to cover various scenarios. It is now common to see definitions for tiny images even where they will never be downloaded.

## The auto value to the rescue

With the new `sizes="auto"` value, the browser automatically calculates the required image width based on the current page layout. Instead of writing complex calculations and media queries, you leave all the math and calculations to the browser itself.

### Proper usage and syntax

For the `sizes="auto"` attribute to work correctly, the image has to be lazyloaded via the `loading="lazy"` attribute. The browser must first process the page layout to determine the exact dimensions reserved for the image before downloading the optimal file from the options in srcset.

```html
<img
  src="image-800.webp"
  srcset="
    image-400.webp 400w,
    image-800.webp 800w,
    image-1200.webp 1200w,
    image-1600.webp 1600w
  "
  sizes="auto, 100vw"
  loading="lazy"
  width="800"
  height="600"
  alt="Example"
>
```

* We no longer need to manually describe breakpoints to the browser. Thanks to auto, it can use the actual image width in the layout.

* The value 100vw serves as a fallback for browsers that do not support auto. For a more precise fallback, you can also use your original set of rules.  
    
* The loading="lazy" attribute is mandatory for auto mode.

### It's far from perfect, though

Auto mode cannot be used universally. For instance, an [LCP image](https://pagespeed.one/en/metrics/lcp#what-is-the-lcp-element?) that we want to load with high priority must still be handled manually.

Measurements and research also show that at a typical phone viewing distance (25–30 cm), the human eye stops distinguishing individual pixels once display density exceeds 300 to 350 PPI.  
![][image1]

*Source: [https\://stackoverflow.blog/2022/12/27/picture-perfect-images-with-the-modern-element/](https://stackoverflow.blog/2022/12/27/picture-perfect-images-with-the-modern-element/)*

A well-compressed 2x image displayed on a 3x screen is completely indistinguishable for 99% of users from a heavy 3x original. Auto mode does not account for this fact and downloads the image based strictly on device PPI.

Now imagine how great it would be to adapt image sizes to current network conditions as well. Unfortunately, we aren't quite there yet.

## Conclusion

Although `sizes="auto"` is not a silver bullet, it addresses the vast majority of problems we face today with responsive images. The rest can be handled individually where closer optimization efforts make sense.

It is time to stop pretending that our hand-written estimates are better than the information available to the browser itself.
